title: Robert Pattinson Says ‘The Batman 2’ Is ‘So Ambitious’ and a ‘Different Take’ on the Franchise: ‘It’s a Real Left Turn From the First’
description:
Robert Pattinson is opening up about “The Batman: Part II” — and how it is a totally “different take” on the franchise than the first film was.

	“I
body:
Robert Pattinson is opening up about “The Batman: Part II” — and how it is a totally “different take” on the franchise than the first film was.

	“It’s so ambitious. I mean, I sort of said the other day on something that the first one was a different take on a Batman movie, and this one is another,” he told Collider in a recent interview. “It’s a real left turn from the first one, but somehow it keeps elements of the kind of feel of it. But it just feels really ambitious, and I’m excited to see how it turns out.”
	

	Set to hit theaters on Feb. 18, 2028, “The Batman Part II” is Matt Reeves’ follow-up to 2022’s “The Batman,” in which audiences were first introduced to the “Primetime” star as Bruce Wayne. Scarlett Johansson and Sebastian Stan will star alongside Pattinson in the film, along with supporting cast members Charles Dance, Brian Tyree Henry and Sebastian Koch. Still, the film’s plot details remain under wraps.


	Variety previously reported that Reeves completed the sequel’s script in June 2025, though the film was originally announced in 2022 — just a month after the first film debuted in theaters. When “The Batman Part II” premieres, it will have been six years since the first did.

	DC Studios co-chief James Gunn previously defended the release delays by explaining how it’s “fairly common” for big-budget titles to have lengthy gaps before a sequel is released.

	“To be fair, a 5-year gap or more is fairly common in sequels,” Gunn wrote on Threads last year. “7 years between ‘Alien’ and ‘Aliens.’ 14 years between ‘Incredibles.’ 7 years between the first two ‘Terminators.’ 13 years between ‘Avatars.’ 36 years between ‘Top Guns.’ And, of course, six years between ‘Guardians Vol 2’ and ‘Vol 3.’”

title: Sister Group Strikes Partnership With Branded Entertainment Company Common Interest, Makes Minority Investment
description: Sister Group, Jane Featherstone and Elisabeth Murdoch‘s ever-growing transatlantic powerhouse, has entered the branded entertainment business by for
body:
Sister Group, Jane Featherstone and Elisabeth Murdoch‘s ever-growing transatlantic powerhouse, has entered the branded entertainment business by forging a strategic partnership with London-based company Common Interest, in which it has also taken a minority investment.

	The partnership with Common Interest, the communications and entertainment group founded by Anthony Freedman, brings together what it describes as “brand creativity, entertainment execution and access to world-class production talent.”
	

	The two groups are already collaborating on projects with the goal of building a slate of projects that are connected with brand partners from the very start. 


	Founded in September 2023, Common Interest now spans brand experience, entertainment-led communications, cultural intelligence and IP development. The group currently numbers eight companies: 21st Century Brand, Amplify, Baby Teeth, CultureLab, Knock Three Times, Otherway, Seed and Wonder. Baby Teeth, the creative company building entertainment and IP for brands and talent, recently created and produced “Finding Jamie,” a microdrama series for the Jamie Oliver Group in partnership with Life360.

	“We immediately found a cultural and creative kinship with Anthony and the exceptionally talented teams he has assembled across Common Interest,” said Murdoch and Featherstone. “Their deep commitment to entertainment and brand strategies that people actually care about, mirrors the values of creative excellence, authorship and risk-taking intrinsic to Sister. We’re not just aligned on paper, but underway on some great ideas where the potency of that combination is very apparent.”
	

	The partnership comes at moment the two companies describe as “structural change,” with brands now welcomed into the entertainment industry conversation from the early stages of development and as audiences increasingly “embrace brand-led content and entertainment across a variety of formats.”

	“Advertising is looking for new ways to reach audiences, and entertainment has never been more open to working with brands as a genuine creative partner,” said Freedman, Founder and CEO of Common Interest. “Each needs what the other has, and the appetite for that is already visible, from Barbie to LEGO to Kraft Heinz’s new partnership with Disney. This partnership is more than a meeting of minds, it’s a real commitment from both sides, to prove that brands can be part of shaping entertainment without compromising on what audiences love.”

	The Sister Group currently spans companies across TV and film (Sister Pictures, Dorothy St Pictures, Yes Yes Media, Locksmith Animation, South of the River, Unanimous Media), podcasting (Campside Media), publishing (Zando, AWA), music and live experiences (KOKO), and digital-first production (After Party Studios). The Group recently announced a partnership with journalist and broadcaster Amol Rajan as the producer and distributor of his new Creator Economy venture.

	The deal with Common Interest was managed by Chris Fry, COO and CFO, Sister Group and Common Interest group’s chief financial and operating officer Deepa Shah.

title: Argonon Unveils Major Leadership Changes as Amanda Goddard Upped to President and Global CEO
description: Argonon, super-indie production group behind shows including “The Masked Singer U.K.,” has unveiled its biggest leadership changes since it was foun
body:
Argonon, super-indie production group behind shows including “The Masked Singer U.K.,” has unveiled its biggest leadership changes since it was founded in 2011. 

	Amanda Goddard, previously chief commercial and legal officer for Argonon, has been promoted to president and global CEO with a worldwide strategic remit across Argonon and its seven production companies. Goddard takes over from Argonon founder James Burstall, who has held the role of CEO for 15 years since launching the group and now becomes executive chairman across the group. 
	

	Meanwhile, Matt Widmayer, formerly CFO for Argonon USA takes on a new role as global CFO for Argonon, splitting his time between the U.K. and U.S., and Hasham Khan of ABP Advisory becomes board consultant.


	 “Our sector is changing at breakneck pace; a restless state of constant evolution is the single most important mindset in a creative business,” said Burstall. “As platform agnostic storytellers whose content reaches millions of people across the world, we must be fearless, experimental, risk-taking and open to radical change to keep us at the cutting edge. Today’s announcement of a brand-new world class leadership team lays the foundations for an exciting future.”

	The senior leadership team changes coincide with several new strategic initiatives across Argonon. The group is actively investing in digital and self-publishing content to build new IP and reach new audiences, exploring partnerships across the nations and regions, investing in its New York hubs, developing new high tech post facilities to support its London labels, and accelerating its AI capabilities. The group is also developing new innovative funding models to support IP creation and investment in content.
	

	Alongside leading the group’s global legal operation, Goddard has helped drive the group’s diversification strategy, using Argonon’s extensive IP library of over 5,800 hours of content to create and grow commercial revenues across brand partnerships, sponsorship, FAST, digital and podcasts. She has also has introduced new content funding and co-funding strategies, call for a more supportive U.K. tax environment for producers and overseen and developed Argonon’s AI strategy and policies.

	“After 15 years leading Argonon’s operations across the UK and US, I am excited to hand over the CEO reins to Amanda, who has demonstrated astute commercial acumen, strong leadership and emotional intelligence since joining Argonon in 2019,” said Burstall. “Her reputation, industry knowledge and strategic vision make her the natural choice to lead Argonon into its next chapter, and I will continue to work closely with her as executive chairman.”

	Added Goddard: “I am proud and excited to step into this new role, working with visionary leaders and talented teams across our global business. Argonon was founded to create an independent platform for talent to be agile and brave, both creatively and commercially, and that enduring spirit is embedded in our culture today. Our world class production companies produce diverse, platform-agnostic content that reaches audiences across the UK and in more than 160 countries, creating employment, economic value and social impact.”

schema.headline: Argonon Unveils Major Leadership Changes as Amanda Goddard Upped to President and Global CEO

title: ‘Fluorescent, Dirty and Sexy’: Eire Cid’s ‘The Imaginary Kings’ Presented at Madrid Film School (ECAM) Incubator
description: Of the five projects at the 9th Incubator program of the Madrid Film School (ECAM), Eire Cid’s debut feature “The Imaginary Kings” (“Los Reyes Imagi
body:
Of the five projects at the 9th Incubator program of the Madrid Film School (ECAM), Eire Cid’s debut feature “The Imaginary Kings” (“Los Reyes Imaginarios”) centers on the angst of male urban youth.

	“It is an irreverent and visceral project, with a stylized, anti-naturalistic aesthetic. Fluorescent, dirty and sexy, heavily influenced by urban culture,” Cid tells Variety.


	The story revolves around Rude, a tattooed teenager living with his father in a working-class  neighborhood. Sensitive yet volatile, he embodies a masculinity that is both aggressive and fragile. Haunted by the sudden death of his pal El Rubio, Rude drifts through trap music, betting, fights, porn and poppers. When he falls for Valeria, she makes him happy but also forces him to confront his grief.
	

	“However, he is unable to connect with his own pain and vulnerability, and to do so, he will have to break,” Cid explains.

	“At the heart of the story is doubt and the possibility of change. That is why we also call it a ‘coming-of-empathy’: a journey toward empathy, much like the one I experienced while writing characters I initially hated as a feminist, but ultimately came to understand,” she says.

	For producer Bea Villar of Brava, “Los Reyes Imaginarios” is a film primarily “for teenagers whose stories are rarely told … and that is at the heart of Brava.“

	“From the beginning, Eire and I shared the same goal: to connect with young people at a time when dangerous ideas about what it means to be a man are resurfacing and to open a dialogue around them,” she noted, expressing her admiration for how Cid stepped outside of her comfort zone to tell this story.
	

	“The setting is also fundamental: a working-class neighborhood in Vigo surrounded by betting shops and bars, with the port cranes in the background. The choice of Vigo was not accidental. Like other European port cities, it carries the legacy of declining industrial masculinity. In many ways, the city reflects the film’s male characters, Villar asserts.

	The project itself has been on quite a journey in its development. It participated in the 4th Edition of the Film Academy’s Rueda Program, the inaugural incubation and development program at the Madrid University School of Arts TAI, the Navarra Residency, the AGAG Mentorship Program for Women Screenwriters and the CREA Conecta Lab.

	The writing process was mentored by such acclaimed filmmakers and writers as Alberto Guntín (“Matalobos”), Belén Funes (“A Thief’s Daughter”), Lola Mayo (“Dolemite”), Golden Leopard winner Albert Serra (“Story of my Death”) and Silvia Herreros de Tejada (“La Ruta”).

	Plans are to shoot it late next year in Vigo, a port city in northwestern Spain. “Vigo is pivotal to the story because, like other European industrial cities, it carries the legacy of a frustrated working-class masculinity shaped by the decline of the shipbuilding industry and offshoring,” says Villar. “That heritage is very present in ‘The Imaginary Kings’ as an intergenerational burden.”



	

					‘The Imaginary Kings’

title: MIP London Ending After Two Years as Organizers Launch New Event at London Book Fair
description:
MIP London will not be returning in 2027, with organizers RX France instead launching a new event alongside the London Book Fair.

	Titled MIP Talks
body:
MIP London will not be returning in 2027, with organizers RX France instead launching a new event alongside the London Book Fair.

	Titled MIP Talks, the two-day conference will take place March 16-17, 2027 — concurrent to the book fair — with the aim of “bringing together leading voices from across the increasingly connected worlds of entertainment, media and culture to explore what is changing, what is breaking through and where new opportunities are emerging,” according to a press release.
	

	The inaugural event will be held at London ExCel and focus on the theme “From IP to Fandom — and Fandom to Global Business.” The programming will include “headline conversations, unexpected pairings, global trends and data, cultural insight and case studies,” the release states, all delving into “an entertainment world where traditional boundaries are disappearing, audiences move seamlessly across platforms and experiences, and IP can come from anywhere.”


	“The boundaries of entertainment have all but disappeared,” said Lucy Smith, director of the entertainment division at RX France, in a statement. “IP can come from anywhere, audiences don’t think in sectors and an idea can travel further and faster than ever before. MIP has always been about understanding where the entertainment business is going next. MIP Talks at the London Book Fair takes that curiosity further bringing together the people shaping what breaks through, how fandom is built and where new global businesses are emerging.”

	Added Emma Lowe, director of the London Book Fair: “The London Book Fair is delighted to be working in partnership with the brilliant team at MIP Talks to meld together our fantastic worlds where stories are created, curated and sent out to find ever more fans, more audiences and more homes.”

schema.headline: MIP London Ending After Two Years as Organizers Launch New Event at London Book Fair

title: ECAM Incubator Title ‘The Woodworm’ Explores Female Identity in the Shadow of an Artist Father
description: In “The Woodworm” (“El Corquim”), the feature debut of Laura Obradors, a teenage girl’s search for an identity of her own runs up against the author
body:
In “The Woodworm” (“El Corquim”), the feature debut of Laura Obradors, a teenage girl’s search for an identity of her own runs up against the authority of her father, a successful artist in creative crisis.

	Developed through Madrid’s ECAM Incubator, the project examines the power exercised inside a family and the artistic prestige that can shield it from scrutiny.

	Produced by Sergio Adrià’s Espurna Films, with Sandra Hermida on board as co-producer, the film centers on 17-year-old Clara, whose desire to be seen and loved is complicated by a growing impulse to escape the expectations surrounding her.
	

	“Clara always seems to crave something from the outside world: to be seen, accepted, acknowledged, adored,” Obradors told Variety. “But at the same time she has an internal and contradictory impulse that wants to push her to break free from these attachments and become more independent, mature, and free.”


	Inspired by the life of a close friend, the project grew from the filmmaker’s interest in the conflicting feelings that can coexist in a daughter’s relationship with her father. For Obradors, that relationship also provides an early encounter with the rules and expectations of a wider masculine world.

	“Somewhere between these two polarities is a world that inspired me to make this film — an attitude, an action, where preservation and destruction coexist,” she said.

	Clara grows up within a family structure shaped by power, submission and male pleasure, with few alternative points of reference. Questioning what she has learned about femininity and intimacy means confronting the guilt attached to that questioning.
	

	Her father Ricard’s profession brings another layer to those dynamics. As both a parent and a painter, he has the power to shape a person’s understanding of the world and the images through which that world is represented.

	“For a long time, we’ve seen the artist as a kind of genius and almost a divine figure,” Obradors said. “That idea can sometimes make us forget that artists are also responsible for what they create and for the power they have.” 

	Adrià, whose producing credits include “Upon Entry” and Gerard Oms’ “Away,” was drawn to the decision to place Clara’s experience at the center of the film.

	“It’s not a film about how he deals with his inner demons or impulses: it’s all about her, focusing on the construction of female identity in a hostile and male-dominated environment,” he said.

	That perspective will also inform the film’s visual approach. Adrià describes a world filtered through adolescence, where people, places and situations can appear idealized, magical or unsettling. The beauty of the landscape will sit alongside the cruelty unfolding among the characters.

	Espurna, which Adrià founded in 2023, is developing the project as part of its commitment to auteur-driven, original-language Catalan cinema with international potential. Obradors previously directed the shorts “Si amanece, nos vamos” and “Las chicas,” the latter produced by Espurna.

	At the time of the interview, “The Woodworm” was on its fourth script draft, following participation in Mexico’s Cine Qua Non Lab and ECAM’s La Incubadora. It has received development support from the Catalan Institute for Cultural Enterprises, with selections for Cannes Focus COPRO’ and ECAM Forum’s Films to Come helping broaden its industry reach.

	Obradors said the development process had allowed her to gain distance from the material’s origins, “put reality at the service of the film rather than the other way around.”

	Hermida, whose credits include “Society of the Snow,” “A Monster Calls” and “The Impossible,” mentored the project through La Incubadora alongside director and screenwriter Carlos Marqués-Marcet, who took a new director Goya for “10,000 km.”

	The team is seeking co-producers, distributors and sales agents across Spain, France, Portugal and Belgium, and are in attendance at San Sebastián and will be at Les Arcs Industry Village.
	

	For Obradors, the title offers a way into Clara’s domestic world: an insect weakening a structure from within, and all the while difficult to detect.

	“It’s a space of repression, silent and invisible, where suffering, fear, and guilt live,” she said. “Clara feels like an intruder, especially when she comes into conflict with the different images of herself that have been constructed around her.”

schema.headline: ECAM Incubator Title ‘The Woodworm’ Explores Female Identity in the Shadow of an Artist Father

title: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson’s Comic Chemistry Isn’t Enough to Make ‘Brothers’ a Compelling Show: TV Review
description: “You have all the hallmarks of a world-class politician,” campaign manager Gwen (Lisa Gilroy) tells her client Matthew McConaughey (Matthew McConaug
body:
“You have all the hallmarks of a world-class politician,” campaign manager Gwen (Lisa Gilroy) tells her client Matthew McConaughey (Matthew McConaughey). “However, your Achilles’ heel is that you’ve been a celebrity for so long that your brain has turned into a big old sloppy pile of goo.”

	The literal premise of the Apple TV comedy “Brothers” is that McConaughey and his friend/fellow Texan/erstwhile co-star Woody Harrelson, also playing himself, may be biological relatives, a possibility they explore while shacked up at McConaughey’s Austin-area ranch. (The actors are also credited as co-creators alongside David West Read and showrunner Lee Eisenberg.) But the comic premise is something closer to Gwen’s observation: that beyond their state of origin and a certain folksy charisma, these two besties share the brain disease that is fame, and when together exacerbate each other’s symptoms.
	

	“Brothers” has plenty of scenes that deliver on this “Dumb and Dumber”-adjacent concept. The pair don ridiculous costumes to prove people don’t tolerate their music just because they’re recognizable, and bicker about hunting (country boy McConaughey is pro, vegan Harrelson is con) on a drive in a keyed-up version of the “True Detective” car rides. This platonic — or perhaps filial — chemistry still isn’t enough to make “Brothers” feel like a real show instead of an overlong comedy sketch.


	Take Gwen, who’s consulting McConaughey on a run for governor. The storyline is a nod to the star’s flirtation with political office, which got serious enough in 2022 to necessitate an announcement that he wouldn’t throw his hat in the ring. But it’s mostly a means to give McConaughey’s fictional avatar a more active plot driver than wondering whether he and Harrelson might be related. The gubernatorial bid certainly isn’t there because McConaughey feels the need to articulate any specific political beliefs, a vagueness “Brothers” gently mocks but also indulges. Real-life Texas is in the middle of a highly contentious senate race; TV Texas is a world with no Greg Abbott, nor a president who’s already a cautionary tale in what happens when pop culture and politics collide. Acknowledging either might mean “Brothers” would have to be something weightier and more fleshed-out than a dopey (in a fun way!) hangout.
	

	A reluctance to get messy or in any way unflattering is a common quality of star-driven shows, and it’s seemingly magnified when two of them are portraying themselves. “Brothers” prefers a soft poke to a sharp jab: Harrelson is a pot-smoking hippie who declines AC because he’s “off freon,” but when he makes a passing mention of COVID, it’s not to share his take on masking and vaccines; McConaughey quotes his own Lincoln commercials when giving his son a pep talk, but the greatest insecurity he’ll cop to is caring too much about being a good husband and father.

	Instead of real insight or self-scrutiny, we get surface-level references to the friends’ filmographies. (These callbacks are oddly skewed toward McConaughey’s CV over Harrelson’s, perhaps because the show takes place on his turf.) The “True Detective” theme plays as a character collects samples for a DNA test, while McConaughey lets his son River (Noah Carganilla) borrow his actual car from “Dazed and Confused” to play dress-up. These allusions rarely inspire a reaction stronger than an amused smile, nor do they try especially hard to do so. “Brothers” is content to trade in its dynamic duo’s public images rather than subvert or complicate them, which is fine — though the resulting vacuum is one of several blank spaces where a real sense of purpose could be.

	“Brothers” is, of course, a show about family, and the show populates its ensemble with lightly distorted bizarro versions of the friends’ loved ones. Holland Taylor cakes on makeup and thick layers of twang as McConaughey’s mother, known to all as “Ma Mac,” whose drunken ramblings prompt Harrelson to do some genetic detective work. No one else makes as strong an impression. In particular, the wives — their show names are Valentina (Natalie Martinez) and Joy (Brittany Ishibashi), but their role and function is accurately summed up as “the wives” — are given almost nothing to do besides roll their eyes at their husbands’ antics. Woody and Matthew forgot about Valentine’s Day? Boys will be boys!

	The kids get more stories of their own, though not ones that ever threaten to pull the spotlight away from their dads. The Harrelsons first set out for Austin (in a solar-powered converted schoolbus, of course) after Woody’s daughter Olive (Highdee Kuan) breaks off her engagement. While I’m always happy to see Skyler Gisondo of “The Righteous Gemstones,” who shows up halfway through the season as the ex-fiancé, he’s underused in a role whose definition stops at “clingy drip.” A romance between River and Olive’s sister Kai (Oona Yaffe) — carefully excused with repeated reminders that Kai is adopted, so there’s no way they’re doing incest — is equally thin. “Brothers” has eyes for only one central relationship, and every second spent on satellite pairings sags with infectious boredom.
	

	For long stretches of the midseason, “Brothers” seems to forget about family intrigue and political ambitions entirely to focus on a harebrained scheme of the week. This straight-sitcom setup, with little serialization to speak of, seems to be where the show’s natural instincts lie. But to justify making room in two packed schedules — we’re repeatedly told McConaughey also has a lucrative tequila brand and multiple courses he designed at UT Austin — “Brothers” has to limply gesture at something more. The season’s final moments tease a potential follow-up, complete with a meta crack about “bandwidth for a franchise.” But to produce a sequel, a project ought to know what it is in the first place. “Brothers” never feels like it does.

	The first two episodes of “Brothers” will premiere on Apple TV on Sep. 23, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays.

schema.headline: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson’s Comic Chemistry Isn’t Enough to Make ‘Brothers’ a Compelling Show: TV Review

title: Finnish Film Affair: Survival, Horror, Dystopian Pics Unpacked by Nordic Genre Lab Participants: ‘The Base of Nordic Talent Is Deep’
description: Home to some of the Nordics’ hottest genre talents making waves at top international festivals – Hanna Bergholm and Ilja Rautsi whose respective “Ni
body:
Home to some of the Nordics’ hottest genre talents making waves at top international festivals – Hanna Bergholm and Ilja Rautsi whose respective “Nightborn” and “Red Snow” were snagged by Shudder – Helsinki will no doubt vibrate this week to the beat of some of the most jaw-dropping and entertaining genre projects taking part in the inaugural Nordic Genre Lab.

	“Alma,” a Finnish thriller penned by Rautsi, “Trespassers,” a Swedish “Deliverance” from “Midsommar” producer Patrik Andersson, and “Whistler,” the first-ever Faroese horror pic, are among eight high-end genre films in development to be showcased at the Helsinki Intl. Film Festival’s industry confab Finnish Film Affair, running Sept 23-25.
	

	Between Thursday and Friday, the Nordic Genre Lab titles will be pitched live to 500-plus delegates, attend workshops and receive mentorship from Two Magpies Entertainment’s Claire Willats, former Netflix commissioner, and genre expert Todd Brown, former XYZ Films head of acquisitions.



	

					Claire Willats, Todd Brown, Laura Laaksonen 
									Courtesy of Claire Willats, Miguel Bueno, Ville Juurikkala
	



	Under their former Netflix and XYZ gigs, the two senior industry executives collaborated on the original Norwegian version of “The Trip,” starring Noomi Rapace and Aksel Hennie, and the acquisition of the Netflix hit “The Platform.” Through her London-based banner Two Magpies Entertainment, Willats is attached to Norwegian “Troll” helmer Roar Uthaug’s upcoming supernatural horror “Amara.” As for Toronto-based Brown, his next ambitious genre bet is Johnnie To’s “Two Gun Cohen,” which is in early development.
	

	When approached by head of program Laura Laaksonen to join her in the intensive training venture Nordic Genre Lab, the two international power players signed up, eager to contribute to strengthening the Nordic genre ecosystem and boost the career of emerging genre talent.

	“Nordic genre remains very strong, in my view,” Todd told Variety. “The base of talent is deep, and the Nordics in general do a remarkable job of balancing class and critical quality with audience accessibility. You continue to not only see a high volume of projects at global festivals but also see those perform commercially.”

	However, he argued, “There still isn’t much in the way of institutional knowledge of genre within funding bodies or a way for these creators to really connect, support and learn from one another in the way they can within the arthouse world.” Which is why he’s hoping with his Nordic Genre Lab colleagues “to help fill that gap.”

	Willats, co-founder of the event with Laaksonen, added: “I think there is a huge appetite for Nordic genre in the global market. If you look at streamers like Netflix, “Troll” is still the number one film not in the English language. We are hoping the lab can help draw more focus on the wealth of talent in the Nordics, and we hope to repeat this next year and include Sámi, Icelandic and Greenlandic projects, which are unfortunately not represented this year,” she stated.

	Together with Norwegian producer Einar Loftesnes (“The Tunnel,” “Kraken”), Willats and Brown selected the eight titles out of 29 submissions, based on the originality of the project, quality of the team, the writing and stage of development.

	The finalists represent “an extraordinary range of genre filmmaking, from folk horror rooted in Faroese landscape to dystopian survival thriller in Norway and from animated psychological horror to dark political satire from Finland and more,” said Willats.

	Among the participants, Jón Hammer (“Trom”), producer of Gudmund Helmsdal’s “Whistler,” said, “We set out to make the first Faroese horror feature, and the first in what we hope will become a series of Faroese genre films, so the opportunity to develop ‘Whistler’ further with the guidance and expertise of such strong mentors is incredibly exciting for us.”
	

	Pauliina Piipponen of Finland’s Making Movies, producer of “Alma,” helmed by Pete Riski (“Icebreaker,” ”Dark Floors”) said, “Taking part in the Nordic Genre Lab comes at a very good moment for the project as we’re now moving further into the creative development and the international financing and production strategy.”

	Juha Fiilin (“Joy Eternal”), director and producer of the Finnish anime horror “Echo Chamber,” hopes to build on the program to strengthen his film’s market potential, ink Nordic distribution and global sales. “Horror is a perennially attractive genre, but the recent successes of ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ prove a maturing of the audience. People are ready for high-quality character work in genre films,” he added.

	Nordic Genre Lab is backed by Nordisk Kulturfond, the Finnish Film Foundation and Nordisk Film & TV Fond.

	Full rundown of the Nordic Genre Lab Projects:“Alma” (Pete Riski, Finland)Produced by Academy-Award shortlisted and Golden Globe nomination Making Movies (“The Fencer,” “My Sailor, My Love”), the ambitious €4 million ($4.5 million) project is penned by genre wiz Ilja Rautsi (“Red Snow,” “Nightborn,” “Hatching”).

	Set between two-timelines World War II Finland. We follow Alma (16), who gains telekinetic powers to save her father from the retreating Nazi army in Lapland. Then in the present day, the same character -aged 96- meets her granddaughter for the first time, and they must escape Alma’s past sins, exploring the cost of gaining power.

	“’Alma’ deals with war and its consequences through three generations of women, combining a historical setting with themes of trauma, power and responsibility that feel particularly relevant today,” says Pauliina Piipponen, who produces with Kai Nordberg and Kaarle Aho.

	“Echo Chamber” (Juha Fiilin, Finland)Anime psychological horror penned by Adam Cullen. First pitched at Cartoon Next 2025.“Echo Chamber” combines tone and artistic sensibilities of prestige drama with the anime-inspired spectacle of chilling body horror, viscerally rendered as only hand-drawn animation can deliver it,” says Fiilin of Fiilin Good Films who produces with Debbie Stepgens. “It’s a mature, thoughtful horror where a curse forces together two sisters estranged by their grief, but that curse inadvertently provides the circumstances and opportunities for them to learn what it is like to grieve together. To see that it is bittersweet and healing; not just bitter.”
	

	“Linden Lane 6” (Josefina Rautiainen, Finland)From the prolific It’s Alive Films, behind Oscar submissions “Euthanizer, “The Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic” and Finnish hit “100 Litres of Gold.”

	“It’s a timely and provocative genre film that reverses the traditional roles of men and women in order to explore sexual harassment, manipulation, and abuse from the opposite perspective,” says producer Anita Hyppönen. “By changing these familiar dynamics, the film shows that abuse is often less about desire and more about power and control.”

	“Long Way Home” (Kjersti Helen Rasmussen, Norway)Produced by Njål Lambrechts for Truewest.Character-driven dystopian road movie in which, after an electromagnetic pulse wipes out all electricity across Western Norway, Tea (22) and her neighbor Herman set out on a dangerous journey through a frozen and increasingly lawless landscape to reach her childhood home, confronting both the chaos around them and the darkness within.

	“At its core, it’s a coming-of-age story,” says Rasmussen. The physical journey home becomes an inner journey from dependency to independence, while the society around the characters faces its own test of trust, solidarity and community. The future I portray is both dark and hopeful. Systems will fail and people will fall, but it is in the darkness that we discover the light and what it costs to choose it,” she says.

	“Sauna Diplomacy” (Teemu Niukkanen, Finland)Debut feature from the director of the 2017 Sundance selected short “Fucking Bunnies” and Canneseries winning series “Money Shot.” Produced by Tack Films’ John Lundsten, behind the 2017 Palme d’Or nominated short “The Ceiling.”

	Dark comedy, set in 1970, during the height of Finlandization. A Finnish diplomat is ordered to host a high-ranking Soviet official at his summer cottage for the weekend. What begins as an awkward diplomatic retreat descends into humiliation, manipulation, and psychological power games.

	“The Evil Eye” (Kristian Lidegaard, Denmark)Penned by Kristian Lidegaard and Sissel Dalsgaard Thomsen, produced by Manna Film (“Kalak,” “The Quiet Migration”).

	Online found-footage horror film in which the main character, Oliver, is both the villain and the creator of the film we are watching. Obsessed with Lucas, a successful young swimmer who bullied him as a child, he secretly films and infiltrates his victim’s life, sharing disturbing “films” on a closed online forum until the line between observer and destroyer disappears entirely. “Told entirely through iPhones, POV glasses, surveillance cameras, screen recordings, social media and an uncensored private forum on the dark web, the film is both instantly recognizable and radically unique. As stories of online abuse and violent digital communities surface worldwide, the film’s horror feels contemporary, borderless and disturbingly real,” says producer Maria Møller Kjeldgaard.
	

	“Trespassers” (Johannes Persson, Sweden)From the director of the horror pic “Feed,” starring Molly Nutley, Sofia Kappel. Written by Melina Maraki (“Summer of 1985”); produced by “Midsommar” producer Patrik Andersson, with Mylla Films co-founder Jakob Abrahamsson.

	Backwoods horror-thriller in which four young people from a failed anti-establishment movement travel to the vast wilderness of Northern Sweden to reconnect with nature, but after a river rafting accident leaves them stranded, they discover they are not alone, and not welcome on land controlled by a group that has isolated itself for centuries with its own terrifying beliefs.

	“Whistler” (Gudmund Helmsdal, Faroe Islands)Produced by Outlier Projects’ Jón Hammer (“Trom”), formerly at Zentropa.

	Helmsdal’s “Brother Troll” bowed at 160 festivals and won best short at the Arizona Int’l Film Festival. Survival folk horror from the set on the bird cliffs and grazing lands of the Faroe Islands, where four marine biologists race to catch the last ferry after their guide’s fatal climbing accident, only to find themselves hunted across forbidden grazing land by a reclusive farmer who uses a bone whistle to command a pack of grotesque half-human creatures.

title: Netflix Competition ‘Wonka’s The Golden Ticket’ Is a Ghoulish Misuse of AI Gene Wilder: TV Review
description: In reviewing “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” a competition series from Netflix loosely (and I mean loosely) based on Roald Dahl’s “Charlie and the Chocolat
body:
In reviewing “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” a competition series from Netflix loosely (and I mean loosely) based on Roald Dahl’s “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” it’s tempting to simply copy and paste my write-up of “Squid Game: The Challenge” from nearly three years ago. After all, the shows share similarly misguided concepts. In trying to kickstart in-house IP into a scalable franchise, the streamer fast-tracked an unscripted offshoot that misunderstands and perverts the original story. The point of both the South Korean drama and the beloved children’s book is that forcing human beings — particularly, in the latter case, children! — into lethal competition over scarce resources is, to be blunt, very bad. Any attempt to rerun these social experiments as straight entertainment rather than cautionary tales, even while removing the chance of bodily harm, is poisoned at the root.
	

	But with “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” there’s an extra, macabre twist to this already sinister endeavor. Rather than a human being or even an anonymous narrator, á la “Squid Game,” the competition is hosted by the voice of Gene Wilder, the actor who played the whimsical chocolatier in the 1971 film “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory,” still the character’s most enduring representation onscreen. (No offense to Timothée Chalamet!) Wilder, of course, died in 2016 at the ripe old age of 83 and was not available to record his lines in the flesh. This version of him has been reanimated using artificial intelligence.


	“Wonka’s Golden Ticket” notes in a disclaimer that the production received the permission of Wilder’s estate for this aural resurrection, presumably in exchange for money. Even if the AI voice is legally sanctioned, however, it still invites a host of other questions. Such as: was this really necessary? Could there possibly be more gained from using Wilder’s nasal croon than lost in viewers put off by the manipulation of a dead man’s image (or rather, sound) for a game show? And if Willy Wonka, a textbook case of Peter Pan syndrome who subjects eager kids to sadistic trials, has always had a strong whiff of menace, where’s the line between deliberately evoking that quality and losing control of it entirely?
	

	None of these queries are answered by the first seven episodes of “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” but it’s still possible to puzzle out how we got here. Netflix acquired The Roald Dahl Story Company, which monetizes the late author’s work, in 2021. The company has since greenlit a drama series based on Dahl’s short stories, and while that works its way through the pipeline, “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” can keep Dahl’s work in the zeitgeist — if not exactly for the right reasons.

	To its credit, the production design of “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” is objectively impressive, recreating iconic sets like the chocolate river, the Wonkavision studio and the “half office” while riffing on the theme for new creations. (There’s a shrinking hallway and a beehive-themed room with honey-slicked floors.) Yet the AI Wilder isn’t the only instance of the contemporary and the retro colliding in unpleasantly discordant ways. Challenges are introduced with “Fallout”-style, ‘50s-esque videos that are aesthetically out of place. It’s hard to make the group sleeping quarters associated with shows like “Love Island” feel natural in a fantastical candy facility. Hilariously, the Oompa Loompas are still around, and some are played by actors with dwarfism — but others are of average height, or even unusually large. I can’t say body diversity for orange homunculi was on my representational bucket list, but at least it’s here!

	Contestants navigate this sensory overload in pairs, put through a series of challenges that combine physical duress (getting spun around in a circle) with social gameplay (choosing which competitors are up for “termination”). The cast have clearly been coached to attribute the design of the “tour” to “Wonka,” who’s referred to by a single name like HAL from “2001: A Space Odyssey.” (Not the influence I’d want to evoke if I were using AI as a load-bearing part of my production, but that’s why I’m not in the television business!) Ticket holders — yes, there’s a staged montage where participants pretend to find golden slips in their chocolate bars — also play up the stakes, which leads to ridiculous statements like “Everything became different when my brother was trapped in the gumball machine.”
	

	The prize for enduring all this is $3 million, oddly phrased as “a six-figure income for 30 years.” But for all the talk about life-changing money, nothing in “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” supplants the Wilder voice as the most attention-grabbing element. (The contestants seem perfectly nice, but there are no breakout stars among the ensemble.) The device grows especially chilling when tasked with delivering jokes, or rather, humor-scented snippets of dialogue that lack a human’s je ne sais quoi. A computer can ape Wilder’s tone of voice, but it can’t (yet) intuit comic timing. One imagines Dahl, whose sometimes monstrous characters captured childhood in all its messiness, would be relieved. I hope no one uses AI to try and ask him.

	The first seven episodes of “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” are now streaming on Netflix, with a two-part finale airing Sept. 30.

title: Mariska Hargitay Teases Christopher Meloni’s ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Return Ahead of Season 28 Premiere
description:
It appears Elliot Stabler and Olivia Benson will reunite once again on “Law & Order: SVU” — at least for an episode.

	Mariska Hargitay shared two p
body:
It appears Elliot Stabler and Olivia Benson will reunite once again on “Law & Order: SVU” — at least for an episode.

	Mariska Hargitay shared two photos of herself and Christopher Meloni on the set of the long-running crime procedural to her Instagram on Tuesday, suggesting that the actor had returned to film the show’s 600th episode. The first photo, which showed Hargitay pointing to the back of Meloni’s head, was captioned “Who dat?” while the second selfie showed the two smiling side by side and was captioned “Happy 600…”.
	

	The sneak-peek into Stabler’s return comes nearly a year after Meloni last guested on the hit show — he most recently appeared in the Season 27 premiere of “Special Victims Unit,” which aired in Sept. 2025 — and five months following the announcement that he’d no longer be playing Stabler full-time after the cancellation of “Law & Order: Organized Crime.”


	He first originated the “Special Victims Unit” character in 1999, when the show debuted on NBC, and continued to portray Stabler through its 12th season in 2011. Episode 600 won’t be the first time the star has returned to the franchise as a guest; in 2021, he came back while launching “Organized Crime,” which premiered in 2021 and ran for five seasons before its cancellation.

	On the subject of Meloni’s departure from the show, Hargitay previously told Variety that she “did not want him to leave.” “I tried so hard to broker that, because it didn’t end great with them,” she said. In the same profile, “Special Victims Unit” producer and Wolf Entertainment president Peter Jankowski said that the actor was, at that moment, visiting the show’s base camp at Chelsea Piers for a meeting with showrunner Michele Fazekas; Meloni told Variety that the end of “Organized Crime” represents a closing of the door on Stabler. “It’s like when I left the last time,” he said. “You’ve got to keep moving.”
	

	Since first premiering, the crime show has racked up an impressive 594 episodes. The 600th episode is set to air during the forthcoming Season 28, which will premiere on Oct. 8.

            She said he "loved so deeply, so purely" and was "incredibly romantic and thoughtful."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We broke the story ... Presley died Sunday at a rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica in what police are investigating as a suspected overdose.
      
    
            Presley was only 27 ... and Lexi says she feels "so lucky" to have known him.

title: Dolly Parton's Nephew's Termination Letter Revealed Amid Estate War
description:
Dolly Parton's Nephew
                          Termination Letter Revealed as Family War Rages
body:
Dolly Parton's Nephew
                          Termination Letter Revealed as Family War Rages
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dolly Parton's nephew wasn't just fired as security for the singer's properties ... he was ordered to stay away and told to have his personnel “peaceably vacate the Properties at once” ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained the letter Bryan Seaver received terminating him and his security companies following "changes in ownership of the Dolly Parton properties."
      
    
    
              
                
  
    
            The letter gets right to the point ... telling Seaver that he and his companies were "formally dismissed and terminated and he's not to be on any of Dolly's properties, effective immediately.
      

            According to the letter, replacement services had already been lined up ... and Seaver was instructed to inform his personnel to "vacate the Properties at once."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The letter says this decision was made by the DP Dean Trust Group for "the protection of the Trust and beneficiaries as a whole."
      
    
            It continues to say the co-trustees will be in contact with Seaver about his interest as a beneficiary "in the near future."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, Dolly's professional-property entity, She's Alive, LLC, has filed a lawsuit seeking a temporary restraining order against Seaver.
      
    
            The lawsuit accuses Seaver of threatening behavior and allegedly trying to pressure the company and trusts for money.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Seaver and his team previously told TMZ they were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions" taken after Dolly's death. His team also said they remain committed to protecting her family and legacy.
      
    
            As you know, Dolly died on August 25 at 80 years old ... and Seaver was the one who announced her passing.

title: Mama June's Late Daughter Anna: Widower's Home Allegedly Shot Up With Baby Inside
description:
Mama June's Late Daughter Anna
                          Widower Says Bullets Ripped Through Home
body:
Mama June's Late Daughter Anna
                          Widower Says Bullets Ripped Through Home ...
                          With Newborn Baby Inside
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Mama June's late daughter Anna "Chickadee" Cardwell's widower says his home was shot up in the middle of the night ... claiming his newborn baby was sleeping inside when a bullet tore straight through the child's crib.
      
    
            Eldridge Toney tells TMZ ... he filed a police report after the terrifying incident, which he says unfolded around 2:45 AM Tuesday when someone was going through the family's vehicles, which were parked outside.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            According to Eldridge, the person was spooked by the car alarms and fired at the house while the children were inside.
      

            Eldridge says the bullet ripped through the nursery wall, passed through the crib, and finally stopped in clothing stored inside a closet. Thankfully, no one was injured.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The close call came just weeks after Eldridge and his fiancée, Jessie English, welcomed their first child, Walker.
      
    
            Eldridge thanked Baldwin police for quickly catching a suspect, though he tells us he has no idea who the person is or why his home was allegedly targeted.
      
    
            He told us ... "It's just crazy one of us could have been killed. We definitely had people upstairs looking out for us!"
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Eldridge was married to Anna from March 2023 until she died from stage 4 adrenal cancer that December ... the couple had been together since 2017.
      
    
            Talk about a guardian angel.
